item.title: Argentina's bid to halt oil drilling off Falkland Islands rejected
item.description:
Argentina's bid to temporarily block oil drilling off the nearby U.K.-held Falkland Islands was rejected Saturday by an international tribunal that rules on maritime disputes.
At a special hearing in Hamburg, Germany, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea voted 18-3 against Argentina's request to halt drilling at the Sea Lion offshore oil project in Falkland Islands waters, around 300 miles east of Argentina's southeastern coast.
The dispute over the planned drilling revived memories of the bitter war the two countries fought 44 years ago over the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and which have been a British overseas territory since 1833.
In a joint statement, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves welcomed the decision and urged Argentina to respect the right of the Falkland Islanders, who number around 3,500 people, to "determine their own future" and end its wider economic pressure.
"This outcome is a vindication of the U.K.'s robust legal defence and strategy," they said. "The U.K. has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders."
In its decision on Saturday, the judges ruled there did not appear to be any basis for believing Argentina had jurisdiction, as the tribunal is unable to make decisions based on questions of sovereignty, Agence France-Presse news agency reported.
Buenos Aires had argued the plan violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute over the sovereignty of the islands is resolved.
Argentine President Javier Milei has vowed to penalize companies working on oil production around the islands and argued that the joint U.K.-Israeli operation is a "clear and present danger" to his country's claims over the islands.

item.title: Charity honoring veteran who raised millions with walks to be disbanded
item.description:
A charity set up by the family of a British World War II veteran who raised tens of millions by walking laps of his garden during the coronavirus pandemic has applied to be disbanded, two years after the country's charity watchdog found "repeated" financial misconduct.
An application to have the charitable company created in honor of Capt. Tom Moore removed appeared Friday on the register of Companies House, the official U.K. government executive agency that maintains the public register of British companies, including charitable ones.
Moore, who died in 2021 at 100 years old, raised almost 39 million pounds, or $49 million, through his daily walks in his yard, inspiring people across the U.K. who followed his exploits in daily TV updates during the early weeks of the pandemic. All of the money he raised was donated to Britain's National Health Service.
Captain Tom Moore, 99, poses with his walker while walking a lap of his garden on April 16, 2020.
JUSTIN TALLIS/AFP/Getty
"That's a lot of dollars — isn't it?" Moore told CBS News in 2021.
Moore was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in July 2020 during an outdoor investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle, in recognition of his huge charity efforts. He also received about 125,000 cards from the public for his 100th birthday and participated in a charity music single that saw him become the oldest British No. 1 artist ever.
Following the success of his fundraising, his family established the Captain Tom Foundation to continue his fundraising efforts. However, the charity was soon embroiled in controversy and Britain's charity regulator concluded in November 2024 that Moore's daughter and son-in-law personally benefited from the charity.

item.title: Gaza strike kills 2 MSF guards whom Israel claims were Hamas fighters
item.description:
Doctors Without Borders, also known by their French acronym MSF, said Friday night two of its staff who worked as guards were killed in an Israeli strike on a clinic in Gaza. The Israeli military accused the men of being Hamas fighters.
"We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen," the humanitarian organization said in a post on X. "This is a direct hit on MSF," it added.
In the statement, MSF also said its premises are marked with logos and its locations are communicated to the Israeli military.
"We stand in solidarity with the families and loved ones of our colleagues. We call for accountability," the statement said.
In response, the Israeli Defense Forces named the two men killed as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, and claimed they were terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.
Palestinians attend the funeral ceremony of Ahmed Abu Hasira.
Ali Jadallah/Getty Images
"While also serving as terrorists, the two worked as security guards at a clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders (MSF). This is another example of the Hamas terrorist organization embedding itself within international organizations," the IDF said in a statement released on Friday.
The Israeli military also disputed the claim that MSF facilities were targeted in the attack, claiming that no damage was caused to medical infrastructure. It added that it had used precision munitions and aerial surveillance to minimize "the expected harm to civilians."
MSF say the deaths bring the total number of their workers killed in Gaza to 17.

item.title: Spain's election could bring the far-right to power for 1st time in decades
item.description:
Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday in a snap election that could see another major European country swing to the political right, as socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez battles to retain power amid mounting public discontent over housing, immigration and corruption.
Sánchez, one of Europe's most prominent left-wing leaders, has increasingly positioned himself as a political counterweight to President Trump on the world stage. He has defied Mr. Trump's demands over NATO defense spending, penned an opinion piece in The New York Times defending migration and denouncing "MAGA-style leaders" and cultivated ties with prominent figures on the American left, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
But at home, Sánchez faces a growing challenge from the center-right People's Party, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, and the nationalist, anti-immigration Vox party, led by Santiago Abascal, which could together form Spain's most right-wing government since the country returned to democracy following the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez gives a speech in the Spanish city of Ceuta, following an attempted sea crossing by migrants from Morocco, on July 31, 2026.
La Moncloa (Spanish Government)/Handout/Anadolu/Getty
A country divided
Housing has become a defining issue of the election, with soaring rents and property prices fueling widespread public anger.
On the same day Sánchez met Mamdani in New York City, 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years. Her landlord had sought to more than triple her monthly rent to $1,900, or 1,650 euros.

item.title: U.S. forces disable commercial ship that allegedly tried to breach Iran blockade
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: U.S. forces used precision munitions to disable a commercial vessel that allegedly tried to breach the American blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command said Friday. The U.S. military said the ship's crew was given multiple warnings before the strike, and that crew members were unharmed.President Trump said Thursday that victory in the war with Iran would be achieved "whenever I want it," and that he is giving the Islamic Republic's regime "a chance to be smart," though he said he doubts they will take it.Mr. Trump also downplayed the importance of Russia and China's intelligence sharing with Iran after multiple reports that Tehran's allies have helped it target U.S. military assets in the Middle East.
New Updates
5:26 AM
Saudi, Houthi forces trade strikes
Saudi Arabia said Saturday it shot down a cruise missile targeting the capital Riyadh, after Houthi media reported Saudi strikes on Yemen.
A Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has been regularly bombing areas controlled by the Iran-backed group since Yemen's civil war reignited over the summer.
In response, Houthi fighters have been targeting the oil-rich kingdom almost daily, hitting energy facilities, airports and Riyadh's financial district.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards the Riyadh region," Saudi coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Malki wrote on X.
It came as Houthi news agency Saba reported a Saudi attack on Yemen's capital Sanaa, which the fighters control.

item.title: 25-year sentence sought for former chef who aided 14 suicides
item.description:
Canadian prosecutors on Friday requested a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold poison to help people die by suicide, stressing his victims were largely young and experiencing mental distress.
Former chef Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to aiding 14 suicides in Canada, but he has admitted to selling his so-called suicide kits globally through a series of online forums.
Prosecutors had also charged him with murder but, citing a lack of evidence, agreed to withdraw the more serious accusations in exchange for Law pleading guilty to lesser offenses.
That decision drew widespread condemnation, notably from friends and family of victims who believed Law was directly responsible for killing their loved ones, but prosecutors maintained they would still seek a stiff penalty.
"An appropriate global sentence to impose in this matter is 25 years less (time already served)," Crown prosecutor Katie Doherty told the court.
Courts often use comparable cases in determining sentencing, but Doherty noted there is "no case even remotely similar to Mr Law's conduct."
The Canadian public was shocked when the breadth of Law's operation was revealed following his arrest.
Kenneth Law pictured in a handout photo from Canadian Police.
Peel Regional Police
He sold poison to people in at least 41 countries, including China, France, and Brazil. He sold 330 packages to people in the United Kingdom, according to an agreed statement of facts signed by the defense and prosecution. There, 79 deaths are linked to him, according to Canadian prosecutors.

item.title: U.S. opens hotline for tips about cartels, angering Mexico
item.description:
Mexico's president has blasted the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of "interference" and not doing enough to fight fentanyl and corruption inside their own borders. President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday the country's foreign ministry has lodged a formal complaint with U.S. Ambassador Ron Johnson.
"We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," she said in her daily news briefing.
Sheinbaum, in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs.
"The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, pointing to the AP report. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups."
"It's clearly an act of interference," Sheinbaum added.
Imagine, she mused, if Mexico "opened a WhatsApp service for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the U.S. government view that?"
Sheinbaum's angry response comes less than 24 hours after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the tip lines on his X account, encouraging Mexicans to denounce members of criminal networks in Sinaloa state, the corrupt officials who support them and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism.
"Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter," Cole said, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.

item.title: Zelenskyy: Trump calling Putin a friend like calling Hitler a friend
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe's future financial commitments to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy said in an interview with CBS News partner BBC News Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Mr. Trump calling Putin "my friend" at a recent summit in China as "strange" because the Russian leader is "an aggressor and a killer."
"He can't be a friend," Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to Adolf Hitler being viewed as a friend during World War II.
The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies including Israel.
In the BBC interview, Zelenskyy called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the U.S. to show both "power and respect."
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor ... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he told the BBC.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Mr. Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend ... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelenskyy and Putin. You know ... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."
